topic: The left-digit effect: why $2.99 feels cheaper than $3 (30-second sample)
method: Peer-reviewed papers (abstracts and NBER working paper summaries) cross-checked with press summaries.

claims.claim: In five experiments, Thomas and Morwitz (2005) showed that a price ending in 9 is judged as smaller than a price one cent higher when the leftmost digit changes, as with $2.99 against $3.00: people anchor on the left digit.

sources.title: Thomas, M. & Morwitz, V. (2005) Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition. Journal of Consumer Research 32(1):54-64
sources.quote: nine-ending prices are perceived to be smaller than a price one cent higher ... only when the leftmost digits of the prices differ (e.g., $2.99 vs. $3.00)

claims.notes: Replication: robust in lab and field (see C2).

claims.claim: In more than 22 million wholesale used-car sales, prices dropped sharply at each 10,000-mile odometer mark; cars just over a mark sold for roughly $150 to $200 less than cars just under it.

sources.title: Lacetera, N., Pope, D. G. & Sydnor, J. R. (2012) Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market. American Economic Review 102(5):2206-36
sources.quote: over 22 million wholesale used-car transactions ... large and discontinuous drops in sale prices at 10,000-mile thresholds

sources.title: NBER Digest summary of Lacetera, Pope and Sydnor
sources.quote: [summary] prices just over a 10,000-mile threshold were $150 to $200 lower

claims.notes: Retail replication by Busse et al.; German listings replication.
